events_chronological: In the schoolroom of a great country house, a girl of thirteen asks her tutor what a carnal embrace is, having overheard talk about him and a guest's wife in the summerhouse.
A minor poet challenges the tutor to a duel over his wife, and the tutor talks him out of it by promising to praise his verses.
The lady of the house quarrels with her landscape designer over his scheme to replace the park with an artificial wilderness and a hermit's cell.
The tutor writes a savage notice of the poet's book while a celebrated aristocrat staying in the house borrows volumes from the library and quits the country.
The poet and a naval officer sail for the tropics with the poet's wife, and the poet dies out there of a monkey bite.
The girl works out a method of drawing natural shapes by repeated calculation, and grasps that heat only ever travels one way.
The night before she turns seventeen she asks her tutor to teach her to waltz, and kisses him.
She dies that same night when her bedroom catches fire.
The tutor becomes the hermit of the estate and fills the cell with calculations until he dies in it.
In the present day a writer works in the same room on a book about that hermit and the collapse of Romantic thought.
An academic arrives hunting a scandal and concludes that the celebrated aristocrat shot the poet in a duel and fled abroad because of it.
A biologist in the family is fitting a repeated-calculation model to two centuries of game records kept in the house.
The academic announces his theory in a public lecture and is taken up by the newspapers.
The biologist recognises that the mathematics in the dead girl's exercise book is a version of what he is doing himself.
The writer proves the poet died abroad of a monkey bite, and the academic's theory collapses in public.
The writer identifies the hermit from a figure sketched into the designer's book of plans.
In the final scene the two centuries occupy the room at once, and both couples waltz among each other's papers.
nonlinear_category_reason: Two periods share one room and alternate scene for scene, each running forward in its own century, and every modern scene decodes the earlier one it follows.
syuzhet_notes: The scenes alternate between the early nineteenth century and the present, each moving forward in its own time, until a final scene in which both periods are on stage at once. Every modern scene works on the evidence the historical scene before it has just produced, so the pairing is explanation rather than contrast.
fabula_notes: The chronology of the earlier strand is fixed by dates in the documents the play itself quotes. The hermit's identity and the girl's death are established only in the modern strand, though the events belong where they are placed here.
